candidates.title: Thinking Harder Doesn't Lead to Better Choices: Reasoning Effort Increases the Confidence but Not the Correctness of LLM Shopping Agents
candidates.content: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous shopping agents that process multimodal product listings (consisting of visual and text data) and recommend purchases on behalf of consumers. Naturally, one might assume that models with more thinking power would make higher-quality purchasing decisions. To test this belief, we ask two questions about such agents: does asking a model to think harder make it choose better products, and does the confidence it reports tell us the likelihood it may be wrong? We benchmark ten frontier models on three product-choice benchmarks built from WebShop, Amazon's SQID and Wayfair's WANDS platforms to see if LLMs with more thinking power actually make better-quality product purchase decisions. Across all three benchmarks, we found that increasing the thinking effort does not increase decision quality in a statistically meaningful way. The same change in thinking effort raises stated confidence at a statistically significant level, so extra thinking buys confidence rather than correctness. candidates.title: The Resolution Hypothesis: Agent Evolution's Key Is Identifying Improvements
candidates.content: Agent evolution follows a simple loop: a proposer writes candidate artifacts (prompts, skills, memories) and selection accepts those that score higher. This loop has shown promise, yet practitioners face a puzzle: methods trade wins across papers, and evolution often fails to bootstrap on certain tasks. We trace this puzzle to the Resolution Hypothesis: agent evolution stalls not because methods fail to propose better artifacts, but because noisy evaluations cannot reliably identify them. Across seven evolution methods and six models (over 10M LLM calls), we find support for the hypothesis at both levels where evaluation scores are used. At the candidate level (choosing artifacts), helpful candidate artifacts exist, but selection is no better than random at telling them from harmful ones, so errors accumulate across rounds. At the method level (ranking methods), typical margins of a few percentage points are smaller than the difference between two independent runs of the same method, so published rankings often rest on luck. candidates.title: Learning Anisotropic Prediction Targets for Flow Models
candidates.content: Flow-based generative models are trained on a hand-chosen prediction target, such as the velocity, the noise, or the clean data. This choice strongly affects training and sample quality. We introduce Anisotropic Flow Models (AnisoFlow), which replaces a fixed prediction target with a fully learnable one. AnisoFlow learns to scale the noise component of the target anisotropically, assigning a separate nonnegative weight to each direction in a jointly learned basis. A closed-form map recovers the velocity from the network's prediction, leaving the architecture, flow-matching loss, and sampler unchanged. Since recovery is exact, training optimizes the target purely to make it easier for the network to predict. We theoretically analyze the resulting prediction error and predict that the preferred noise weight in each direction scales near-linearly with data variance, in agreement with the weights learned empirically in pixel space. AnisoFlow improves FID from 1.90 to 1.55 over the JiT baseline on ImageNet 256times256, by learning only the prediction target, without representation alignment or architectural changes. candidates.content: External sandboxes for coding agents I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine. I worked on this project with Prime Radiant , the AI research lab behind Superpowers and other projects . My post on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the external sandbox pattern, where code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox. To demonstrate this pattern we've released three sandbox server implementations: external-sandbox-v86 runs a Node.js server which then uses v86 to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly. external-sandbox-container is a Python web server which runs the sandbox in Alpine Linux inside an Apple Containers instance. external-sandbox-quicksand is another Python web server, this time using Microsoft's Quicksand sandboxing library, which bundles QEMU and Alpine Linux in a Python package! candidates.title: Fully modified SpyCas9 guide RNAs enable robust genome editing in cells and in vivo
candidates.content: Abstract Precision engineering of CRISPR/Cas9 components has advanced genome editing toward therapeutic applications. Fully chemically modified guide RNAs (gRNAs) have the potential to improve stability and broaden therapeutic delivery strategies. However, extensive chemical modification of CRISPR guides can compromise genome editing activity by disrupting gRNA–Cas9 interactions. Here, we employed an iterative, structure-guided optimization strategy to systematically evaluate chemical modifications throughout SpyCas9 gRNAs. Extending beyond commonly used nucleotide modifications, we incorporated 2′-amino-RNA, 4′-thio-RNA, and extended nucleic acid (exNA) to generate gRNAs in which 90%–100% of nucleotides are sugar- or backbone-modified. Although the performance of individual modification patterns varied among target sequences, we established a repertoire of guides that support robust genome editing in vitro and in vivo . Collectively, these findings provide a systematic framework for rational engineering of heavily and fully modified gRNAs using diverse nucleotide chemistries for nonviral CRISPR genome editing.

candidates.title: Timing of ribosomal RNA modification during eukaryotic ribosome biogenesis
candidates.content: Abstract Ribosomal RNA (rRNA) modifications are critical for ribosome function, influencing rRNA stability, structure, and interactions with ribosomal proteins and transfer RNA. However, the precise timing of modification during the complex process of ribosome biogenesis remains unknown. We address this knowledge gap by analyzing Saccharomyces cerevisiae precursor rRNA (pre-rRNA) through purification of RNA polymerase I and III and Nanopore direct RNA sequencing. Using quantitative RNA modification analyses of distinct pre-rRNA intermediates along the rRNA maturation pathway, we discover the timing of rRNA modifications mediated by small nucleolar ribonucleoproteins (snoRNPs) and other enzymes. All H/ACA snoRNPs act co-transcriptionally to form pseudouridines before 20S and 27SA2 pre-rRNAs are separated, and the same is true for C/D snoRNPs generating 2′-O-methylations. Most modifications, particularly those at the 5′ end of 18S rRNA, are fully installed already in 35S pre-rRNA, however certain modifications in the central and 3′ regions of 18S rRNA are only completed in later stages of ribosome assembly. candidates.title: Conformationally heterogeneous RNA stem-loops enable dimerization-assisted assembly of SARS-CoV-2 Nsp9
candidates.content: Abstract SARS-CoV-2 non-structural protein 9 (Nsp9) is an essential RNA-binding protein, yet the physical principles governing its RNA recognition remain poorly defined. Using NMR spectroscopy, small-angle X-ray scattering, dynamic light scattering, cell imaging, and viral yield-reduction assays, we show that Nsp9 preferentially engages conformationally heterogeneous RNA stem-oops and assembles through dimerization-assisted, multivalent interactions. Structured stem-loops with well-defined conformations and extended single-stranded RNAs exhibit only weak, localized binding. In contrast, the stem-loop-rich host 7SL S domain engages an extended interaction surface across the Nsp9 dimer. A 20-nt RNA hairpin bearing phosphorothioate and 2′- O -methyl modifications recapitulates this binding behaviour and promotes concentration-dependent formation of higher-order Nsp9 assemblies. candidates.content: The use of cyanobacteria as biotechnological chasses is considered a key point in the circular economy due to their scarce growth requirements and its capacity of fixing atmospheric CO2. However, for obtaining the most of their potential, it is often necessary to count with tools that allow the modification of the genetic expression. In this work, we have characterized a molecular toolbox for reliable control of gene expression control through induction or repression in Synechocystis sp. PCC6803 using SEVA plasmids. Different inducible promoters showing a variety of dynamic range, strength and leakiness using GFP our YFP as reporter genes were assayed. On the other hand, we also evaluated the gene repression in cyanobacteria by using CRISPRi technology, which allows to repress the gene transcription in a targeted manner. The vector contains dCas9 (DNase-dead Cas9 nuclease) under the tightly regulated PBADRSW promoter, which combines a theophylline-responsive riboswitch with a rhamnose-inducible promoter. candidates.title: Exponent Polytopes for Abstracting Chemical Reaction Networks into Formal Specification Models for Compositional Design of Biomolecular Circuits
candidates.content: Model based design has shown promise for synthetic biological circuits. However, many approaches remain empirical and limited in scale. Here, we develop specification models from chemical reaction network (CRN) models. These specifications encode assumptions explicitly and guarantees that must be met under those assumptions. Specifically, we show how monomial dominance relations in open CRNs induce polyhedral regime assumptions in logarithmic coordinates. These assumptions give polyhedral assume guarantee contracts that encode system behavior. Further, we show how order of magnitude dominance assumptions can be written explicitly as contract assumptions and used to derive tighter guarantees. We demonstrate two biological circuit design applications: identifying the biological mechanisms that meet the required system-level specification, and screening promoter and ribosome binding site choices to determine expression gains that satisfy a specification through contract composition and refinement. Ultimately, these results provide a path from CRN descriptions of synthetic biological parts to specification-based compositional design.

candidates.title: Transcriptomic data and biomedical literature synergize in finding pharmacologic gene regulators
candidates.content: Abstract Most disorders caused by a deficiency or excess of one gene product lack targeted therapies. Since these disorders can be modeled with a gene overexpression, knockout, or knockdown, drugs that oppose the transcriptomic effects of such perturbations may be promising therapeutic candidates. RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) studies can fuel this drug-prioritization, but their labels, written in plain language, must be annotated manually. Hence, we introduce Signature-based Networks from Automatically Curated Knockout, Knockdown, and Small-molecule Studies (SNACKKSS), which automatically curates gene-disruption and drug-treatment studies from the Gene Expression Omnibus and, in partnership with uniformly computed read count datasets, feeds the labels and RNA-seq data directly into regulatory relationship predictions. Through cross-validation, we show that the predictions from SNACKKSS (specifically, from a variant called “SA4”) make a unique contribution to finding protein-inhibiting compounds, even alongside existing predictors. We demonstrate the benefit of aggregating multiple predictive tools, and provide this powerful ensemble alongside SNACKKSS. Importantly, we advise researcher

candidates.title: Beyond the double-helix: non-canonical nucleic acid structures as drug targets and therapeutics
candidates.content: Abstract Nucleic acids adopt a rich repertoire of non-canonical structures beyond the iconic double helix — G-quadruplexes, i-motifs, triplexes, R-loops, Z-DNA/Z-RNA, and junctions — with roles in genome stability, transcription, replication, and translation. Yet the biological evidence for these conformations varies widely, from direct in vivo validation to largely indirect biochemical inference. We organize this review around a distinctive therapeutic duality: non-canonical structures may serve as molecular targets for small molecules, peptides, and nucleic acid-based modulators, while some are also engineered as therapeutic agents in their own right. For each structural class, we critically assess structural principles, biological evidence, and detection methods, explicitly distinguishing direct in vivo validation from cell-based and biochemical observations and noting the limitations of current detection strategies. Comparing translational maturity across classes through the lens of target versus agent, we identify key challenges — structural selectivity, mechanistic attribution, target engagement, and delivery — that must be resolved to fully realize the therapeutic potential

candidates.title: Can Decision Models Replace LLMs in Real-World Contact Center Classification and Judging Tasks?
candidates.content: arXiv:2611.22949v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Contact center systems often need to make bounded decisions, such as identifying a caller's intent, retrieving the knowledge-base article that answers a query, assessing agent compliance, or judging the output of AI models used in production. Decision models return a typed answer and its probability directly, making them a promising cost-effective alternative to generative Large Language Models (LLMs) in such bounded conversational tasks. However, their effectiveness in real-world contact center applications remains unclear. In this paper, we compare nine decision models against thirteen generative LLMs in zero-shot settings across eight contact center use cases: six classification tasks and two judging tasks. Our experiments demonstrate that many decision models can match the performance of frontier LLMs on contact center classification, and API-based closed decision models achieve this at the lowest per-request cost among the API models we evaluate. candidates.title: VRLLM: Turning LLMs into Powerful Tabular Classifiers
candidates.content: arXiv:2611.22308v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on text, but whether pretrained LLMs are effective for large-scale tabular classification remains unclear, as many previous works demonstrate that LLMs' tabular data classification performance falls behind tree-based models or neural architectures designed for tabular data. At Visa Research, we managed to fine-tune a pretrained Llama 3.2 1B LLM on billions of rows of labeled tabular data and make it outperform a wide array of tabular classifiers and even our competitive production deep learning model. For ease of reference, we refer to the model as the Visa Research LLM (VRLLM). In this paper, we share how we achieved this exciting result, covering data preparation, training recipe, ablation studies of design choices and deployment validation. We also benchmark frontier LLMs on the same task and analyze their prediction behavior across model families and generations. candidates.title: Arabic Safety Alignment as Selective Refusal: An Empirical Study of SFT, DPO, and Guard Calibration
candidates.content: arXiv:2608.29378v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Arabic large language models must refuse harmful prompts without over-refusing benign or sensitive prompts, yet a single refusal rate hides this trade-off. We evaluate it using benign refusal B and harmful-prompt refusal H, where H measures refusal rather than harmful compliance. Across five Arabic-capable models and 130 runs on the full human-written AraSafe set, refusal-only supervised fine-tuning (SFT) collapses toward blanket refusal, whereas selected mixed-SFT configurations reach H = 90% to 93% at B = 14% to 23%; four selected configurations exceed the H = 90% target in all three runs, while Fanar does so in two of three. Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and inference guards change B and H differently across models rather than acting as uniform upgrades. In a blinded 300-response audit, annotator binary-refusal agreement is 89.0% (kappa = 0.78); Qwen3Guard and Aya Expanse 32B reach 88.7% and 91.0% accuracy, respectively, with no conclusive paired difference. candidates.title: HealthCLBench:Evaluating Context Learning in Health Conversations through Controlled Case Clusters
candidates.content: arXiv:2611.22362v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Complex health conversations require answers grounded in individual information and currently valid evidence. We evaluate health context learning: acquiring, integrating, and applying relevant context during inference with fixed model parameters to answer health questions and respond appropriately to changes in facts, evidence, or task goals. To our knowledge, Chinese-language medical benchmarks have yet to systematically combine explicit contextual difficulties, controlled case variations, and member-specific medical criteria for open-ended answers. We introduce HealthCLBench, comprising 328 controlled clusters, 1,103 cases, and 4,931 rubric criteria across medical consultation and everyday health management. Members share backgrounds while evidence, patient states, or task goals change; each has its own medical scoring requirements. A 70-person medical team annotates and reviews the simulated cases and their rubrics. Human review of 700 full-context responses from the original evaluation yields 90.5% pooled agreement with the original automated judgments at the rubric-item level. candidates.title: ARC-2: Continuous Compliance Through Delta Management
candidates.content: arXiv:2611.21811v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: ARC 1 introduced a three-layer governance architecture for autonomous systems comprising model safety validation, cognitive certification (CRAB), and operational authorization (LEA). However, it did not address how compliance should be maintained after deployment. This paper introduces Delta Management, a continuous governance framework that measures deviations between a system's current operational state and its certified baseline, defined as a region rather than a fixed point. Compliance is assessed through continuous monitoring instead of static certification. Four extensions are proposed. First, CRAB evaluation incorporates the worst verified behavioral deviations, with isolated outliers quarantined pending confirmation to prevent unjustified restrictions. Second, a layered trigger taxonomy distinguishes hard safety violations, critical single-dimension failures, correlated multi-system degradation, and risk-weighted composite indicators, each triggering proportionate responses. candidates.title: RIPPLE: Recovery Internalization through Process-Level Policy Learning and Effect-Aware Credit for Long-Horizon Agentic Coding
candidates.content: arXiv:2610.31276v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Long-horizon coding agents can observe a failure and generate a plausible critique yet continue along the same incorrect trajectory. We call this the Critique-to-Action Handoff Gap. We introduce RIPPLE, a recovery-oriented training framework that internalizes process-level guidance into a single self-recovering policy. A prefix-only teacher provides evidence-grounded recovery supervision without access to future actions or terminal outcomes. After lightweight distillation, reinforcement learning assigns stage-specific credit to reflection triggering, diagnosis, and corrective action. Local validity signals gate trajectory advantages so that intermediate recovery decisions do not indiscriminately inherit terminal outcomes. Across four repository-level software-engineering benchmarks, RIPPLE improves the base policy by an arithmetic mean of 4.8 score points, with no auxiliary critic at deployment. Controlled ablations isolate the benefits of local, stage-aligned credit, and matched-prefix interventions show that critique semantics affect subsequent correction. candidates.title: The Economics of AI Foundation Models: Openness, Competition, and Governance
candidates.content: arXiv:2510.15200v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Foundation model developers choose how open to make their models. Greater openness lowers downstream adaptation costs but can also make competing models easier to use. In a two-period model, an incumbent chooses its license fee and openness, a deployer adapts the model for users, and an entrant offers a competing model. Usage builds model-specific experience that lowers the deployer's future adaptation cost, creating a data flywheel that favors continued use of the incumbent. We identify conditions under which optimal openness falls and then rises as learning strengthens. The incumbent moves from full openness and a high fee to restricting openness for retention, then to a low fee that builds enough usage and experience to retain the deployer despite greater openness. A full-openness mandate can induce the incumbent to abandon this low-fee strategy. The higher fee can reduce first-period adaptation despite greater openness. An openness trap arises when this welfare loss exceeds the second-period gain from easier adaptation of the entrant's model. The trap can disappear when experience transfers across models. candidates.title: Cassette-Editor: Shared Timeline Semantics for Human and Agent Editing
candidates.content: arXiv:2610.37690v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Video editing involves tedious manual manipulation across interconnected timeline tracks, motivating automated agents that offload routine work while keeping the project directly revisable by humans. Fixed operation catalogs limit expressiveness, while even a basic trim requires coordinated updates across later clips, attached titles, and transitions. We present Cassette-Editor, an agent harness that unifies manual user gestures and automated agent patches within a shared editing environment. The shared action language expresses the editor's manual content changes, and a common history records committed edits for undo and manual refinement. When the model selects an edit, a state executor automatically derives its downstream consequences, such as shifting later clips and attached titles after a trim, while a validation rulebook enforces structural invariants and returns localized diagnostics for automated repair. To keep the agent grounded as the project evolves, dynamic read operations map transcripts and shot descriptions onto the current timeline. candidates.title: Auditing World-Model Explanations in Retail Forecasting: Faithfulness, Accuracy and Price Response
candidates.content: arXiv:2611.20811v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Forecasting models that read the price and promotion plan explain each forecast as a baseline, what would sell with nothing planned, plus the lift the plan adds, and merchants order stock and plan promotions on that lift. We show that an explanation can pass the checks used to trust it and still be wrong enough to cost money. We define eight checks for any forecaster that states a plan lift, six with a pass rule fixed before any result, and run them on a world model and on LightGBM. In generated store data with known effects, the world model passes the checks of construction, stability, price direction and agreement with sales and with LightGBM, yet when merchants plan into high-demand weeks it states 1.33 to 1.40 times the true lift, and 1.23 to 1.42 times in eight variants of that world; LightGBM overstates it too (1.26, and 1.16 to 1.35). Both still pick the right weeks to promote, but stock ordered to the world model's lift is off by 0.44 to 0.48 of the true lift. candidates.title: FACE: Flow-Guided Angular Channel Estimation Framework for mmWave MIMO Systems
candidates.content: arXiv:2611.21698v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Acquiring accurate channel state information (CSI) is essential for millimeter-wave (mmWave) multi-input multi-output (MIMO) systems. However, it remains challenging due to high-dimensional channels, limited pilot observations, and measurement noise. To address these challenges, we propose flow-guided angular channel estimation (FACE), a novel channel estimation framework based on flow matching, an emerging generative modeling paradigm that learns continuous transport dynamics between probability distributions. FACE exploits the inherent angular-domain sparsity of mmWave channels and incorporates the learned flow matching model as a generative channel prior. Numerical results show that FACE consistently achieves higher channel estimation accuracy than both conventional estimators and diffusion-based generative estimator across diverse channel and system configurations. Moreover, FACE maintains high estimation accuracy with fewer pilot observations and achieves an average achievable rate close to the perfect-CSI benchmark.
